content.text:
**1) VERIFIED (primary/scholarly sources, e.g., Britannica).**[[1]](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Angkor-Wat)[[1]](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Angkor-Wat)

Britannica states that Angkor Wat was constructed in the 12th century (specifically under King Suryavarman II, r. 1113–c. 1150) of the Khmer Empire as a vast funerary temple dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu. It later transitioned to a Buddhist shrine (with Hindu images replaced by Buddhist ones) under King Jayavarman VII (r. 1181–c. 1220), and Theravada Buddhist monks maintained it thereafter. This aligns precisely with the claim of early 12th-century Hindu origins dedicated to Vishnu and gradual conversion to (Theravada) Buddhism by the late 12th/early 13th century onward.[[2]](https://www.britannica.com/place/Siem-Reap)

**Source URLs:** https://www.britannica.com/topic/Angkor-Wat (multiple sections on history and transition); related UNESCO reference at https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/668/ (Angkor site, noting the complex's history).

**2) VERIFIED (consistent reporting across travel and mapping sources).**[[3]](https://www.asiaodysseytravel.com/cambodia/how-to-get-to-angkor-wat.html)

Angkor Wat lies roughly 5.5–8 km (about 3.4–5 miles) north of Siem Reap town center. Drive times are routinely reported as 10–20 minutes by taxi/car (depending on exact starting point in town, traffic, and route), which matches the “roughly a 15-20 minute drive” description.

**Source URLs:** https://www.asiaodysseytravel.com/cambodia/how-to-get-to-angkor-wat.html (explicitly 5.5 km / 10–20 min); https://www.rome2rio.com/s/Siem-Reap/Angkor-Wat (8 km / ~10 min drive).

**3) PARTIALLY VERIFIED / REPORTED (volume and blocks widely cited; height is standard but less directly sourced in the queried encyclopedias).**

- **Volume (~55,000 cubic metres) and ~2 million stone blocks:** Commonly reported in reliable secondary sources drawing from archaeological data (e.g., andesite stone used). No direct contradiction; figures appear consistently.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur)
- **Height (35 m):** This is the standard cited height of the monument (main structure); it aligns with general references but was not explicitly confirmed in the Britannica/UNESCO hits from the searches.

The stone volume/block figures are widely accepted but derive more from archaeological summaries than a single primary UNESCO/Britannica page in the results. No Britannica or UNESCO page directly quoted the exact 55,000 m³ / 2 million blocks in the tool outputs, though the overall scale is consistent with scholarly descriptions of the monument.

**Source URLs (for volume/blocks):** Wikipedia summary of archaeological data (cross-referenced in multiple sites); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur (citing ~55,000 m³ andesite and ~2 million blocks). Height is standard in UNESCO Borobudur listings (https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/592/). Britannica does not appear to host a dedicated Borobudur page with these metrics in the results.
